deep.reconstruction:
The page has no derivations. It holds two unrelated items.

(1) Top two lines, in ink, in Latin: 'Inventis formis, quas functio induere potest, aequationes etiam differentiales, quibus satisfacere potest, facile formantur unde ...' ('Once the forms the function can take have been found, the differential equations it can satisfy are also easily formed, whence ...').
- This is a programmatic sentence, broken off after 'unde'. It belongs to Riemann's approach to the Gauss hypergeometric function. In that approach one first finds the possible 'forms' of the function: its branches and expressions around the singular points 0, 1, infinity, with prescribed exponents (the P-function). Only afterwards does one derive the second-order linear ODE these forms satisfy.
- In modern terms: if y has a two-dimensional space of branches with local exponents (a,a'), (b,b'), (c,c') at 0, infinity, 1 and a+a'+b+b'+c+c'=1, then any two branches y1, y2 determine the ODE through the Wronskian. The equation is det[[y, y', y''], [y1, y1', y1''], [y2, y2', y2'']] = 0. It reduces to the Riemann–Papperitz equation, and to the Gauss equation x(1-x)y'' + (gamma-(alpha+beta+1)x)y' - alpha beta y = 0 after normalising.
- Nothing is computed on this page. The derivation step that 'unde' introduces is not written.

(2) The rest is a heavily corrected pencil draft of an official letter in Kurrent, addressed to 'Ew. Excellenz' (a ministry or curatorial official in Hannover). It concerns the Göttingen professors' widows' fund (Wittwen-Institut / Wittwen-Casse).
- Riemann answers a 'Schreiben vom 15 Dec. v. J.'. He states that a reliable judgement of the fund's solvency needs its future obligations to be set against its probable income. One preliminary is the ratio of widows to members expected in the steady state ('Beharrungszustand').
- He notes that the files before him contain only the balance sheet ('Bilanzrechnung') drawn up by the fund's direction for 1 July 1856. That sheet showed an annual surplus of 3594 Thaler.
- He recalls that the official had wished, during Riemann's visit to Hannover, for such a calculation to be made. Riemann offers to carry it out with the help of Herr Hattendorf[f], provided the preliminary data are collected. He asks for postponement of the report and for guidance on how to obtain the needed statistical notes.
- He closes by announcing remarks on the 1856 balance sheet, which he thinks could easily mislead about the fund's position.
- No actuarial computation appears on this page.
errors: No mathematical steps on the page to check. The Latin sentence is a correct statement of method, but it is unfinished: it stops at 'unde'.

results.what: Methodological statement: determine the many-valued forms (branches and local behaviour) of a function first, then form the linear ODE they satisfy
results.modern_name: Riemann's P-function approach to the hypergeometric equation (Riemann–Papperitz equation)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, 1857 ('Beiträge zur Theorie der durch die Gauss'sche Reihe F(α,β,γ,x) darstellbaren Functionen'); Papperitz 1885 for the explicit general equation

results.what: Draft letter proposing an actuarial assessment of the Göttingen professors' widows' fund (steady-state widow ratio; obligations vs. expected income), mentioning Hattendorff as collaborator
results.modern_name: Actuarial valuation of a pension/widows' fund
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss did the earlier valuation of this fund (1845–51); Hattendorff later worked in insurance mathematics (Hattendorff's theorem, 1868)

deep.surprise_reason: The Latin line restates Riemann's known 1857 P-function philosophy. The letter is biographical and administrative, not mathematical. Riemann's involvement with the widows' fund after Gauss, and Hattendorff's role, are of minor historical interest only.

checkable.asserts: Gauss's 2F1 satisfies the hypergeometric ODE (the equation Riemann derives from the 'forms' of the function).
The second branch x^(1-c) 2F1(a-c+1,b-c+1;2-c;x), with exponent 1-c at 0, satisfies the same ODE, illustrating the 'forms' (branches) of the function.
